chunks: Fadalah ibn Ukeyem from Abdullah ibn Bukayr from Abu Basir from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) used to say in his sermon: 'Cursing a believer is transgression (fisq), and fighting him is disbelief (kufr). Consuming his property is disobedience (ma'siyah), and the sanctity of his property is like the sanctity of his blood.'

key_terms.فِسْقٌ: Transgression or moral deviation, lesser than disbelief

ai.seo_question: What are the spiritual and legal consequences of cursing or fighting a believer according to the Prophet's sermon?
ai.summary: This hadith from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) highlights the Prophet’s frequent emphasis on the sanctity of the believer’s honor and property, framing social transgressions within a hierarchy of spiritual severity. It underscores the Shia scholarly view that while cursing is a major sin (fisq), physical conflict escalates to disbelief (kufr), reflecting the gravity of violating the believer's rights. The comparison of wealth to blood emphasizes the economic dimension of dignity in early Islamic society.

en.shaykh-tahir-ridha-jaffer: 23.Faḍālah narrated from ʿAbdullāh ibn Bukayr, from Abū Baṣīr, from Abū Jaʿfar (a) who said, “The Messenger of Allah (ṣ) used to say in his sermon, ‘Cursing a believer is transgression and fighting him is disbelief. Consuming his property [without permission] is a sin and his property is as inviolable as his blood.’”
